full_judgment:
K. Hossain, J.In this revisional case a fundamental question of law is involved in that whether in a suit for declaration simplicity to immovable property without appropriate consequential relief, an application for appointment of Receiver is maintainable. Since the suit is pending and facts agitated by the contending parties are to be adjudicated upon on merits we refrain from making a detailed reference to them except the fact touching on the point before us. It appears that a dispute cropped up over possession of the suit land between the plaintiff and the defendants which led toot he initiation of a criminal proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It culminated in an order under section 146 of the Code. The, Magistrate could not come to any conclusion as to which of the contending parties was actually in possession of the suit property. He attached the property; appointed a Receiver and directed the parties to get their title decided in a civil court. The plaintiff was the first party and he also instituted the present suit for declaration of title simplicity. He filed an application, on certain allegation against the Receiver appointed by criminal court, and wanted to upset. the arrangement of the Receiver appointed by the criminal court. The Trial Court allowed the prayer and it was challenged in appeal by the defendant petitioner. Being unsuccessful he has come before this court with a question of law as set out above. Mr. Moinul Huq challenges the jurisdiction of the court in suit for declaration of title simplicity to immovable property to appoint a receiver. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider says he has. The rival contentions may be considered. 

 (2) The court should not appoint a receiver except upon proof by the plaintiff that prima facie he has very excellent chance of succeeding in the suit. 

 (3) Not only must the plaintiff show a case of adverse and conflicting claims to property, but he must show some emergency or danger or loss demanding immediate action and of his own right he must be reason by clear and free from doubt. The element of danger is an important consideration. A court will not act on possible danger only; the danger must be great and imminent demanding immediate relief. It has been truly said that a court will never appoint a receiver merely on the ground that it will do no harm. 

 4. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party referring to eases reported in 48 C.W.N. 49; and 15 C.W.N. 78 says that it can be so done. A discussion of these authorities is not called for, as they do not relate to the question before us, and in our opinion they have not much relevancy. The court, no doubt, as we have seen has the jurisdiction but that jurisdiction is dependent upon the frame of the suit arid the reliefs sought. The plaintiff must frame his suit in a manner as to clothe the court with the jurisdiction to decide both the title and possession of the suit property. Has the plaintiff so framed his suit? It is a suit for declaration of Title simplicity without any prayer for either confirmation of possession or recovery of possession to immovable property. Therefore the court is not called upon to deal with the question of possession. In this suit the question of delivery of possession will arise, but on the frame of the suit, that relief could not be either asked for or granted. Receiver therefore could not be appointed. 

 5. Mr. Haider however submits that since the property is attached under section 146 Cr. P. C. on the declaration of plaintiff's title, he will get possession from the Criminal Court. The argument suffers from approbation and re-probation. By praying appointment of receiver by the civil court, as section 146 C.P.C. says, criminal court will lose its possession since receiver appointed by it will be discharged. But then civil court because of the frame of the suit cannot deliver possession to the plaintiff. If the plaintiff's prayer is allowed, both the criminal and the civil courts will lose their jurisdiction to deliver possession to successful party. Such a stalemate cannot be contemplate in law nor can a court be allowed to create such a deadlock. We are not impressed by the argument of Mr. Haider.
